---
title: "Manual examples and pattern matching"
subtitle: "Type a small set of messages by hand. Examine a text pattern."
description: "Type small examples by hand and use them to find dates, email addresses, and order numbers in R."
categories: [source data loading, regular expressions, testing]
---

Near the end of a support shift, a worker needs to connect incoming messages
with the right orders. One message may contain two order numbers, another may
contain an email address, and most contain neither. Reading a small inbox is
easy. Processing hundreds of messages makes missed and mistaken
matches more likely.

The worker types five messages by hand rather than exporting the full inbox.
Every expected answer fits on the screen. Some examples should fail.
Manual entry also avoids changes that another system might make to the text.
We will use these examples to create a pattern and examine its limits.
Then we will hide an address before sharing the messages.

::: {.callout-tip}
## What you will learn

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

- search for an exact word or phrase.
- describe a set of values such as order numbers or dates.
- extract and replace matching text.
- create checks for mistakes from hand-written examples.
:::

```{r}
#| include: false

options(warn = 2)
stopifnot(identical(getOption("warn"), 2L))
```

## Make a small example set

The five messages contain different cases and are short enough for visual
inspection. In R, `c()` combines values into a collection called a
**vector**. The arrow `<-` saves that vector under the name `messages`.

```{r}
library(stringr)
library(tibble)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)

messages <- c(
  "Alex likes to play guitar.",
  "Email support@example.com before 17:30.",
  "Order IDs: R-1042 and R-1043.",
  "The café opens on 2026-08-28.",
  "No identifiers here."
)

messages
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(length(messages), 5L),
  identical(messages[3], "Order IDs: R-1042 and R-1043.")
)
```

R prints all five messages. The number in square brackets at the left marks the
position where that line of output begins.

The messages are English. Web and publishing tools identify English with the
BCP 47 language tag `en`. The language matters for two later rules. The order ID
rule assumes ASCII digits, and the `^ERROR:` rule assumes a Latin-script label
in capital letters. These assumptions do not apply to Arabic-Indic digits or a
script without case.

The email and date patterns can apply more broadly because they describe text
structure. The date rule still assumes a Gregorian calendar with the largest
unit first.

## Search for exact text

Use an exact search when the required text is known. Here we search for
`"café"` before introducing a flexible pattern.

```{r}
cafe_message <- str_subset(messages, fixed("café"))

cafe_message
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(cafe_message, "The café opens on 2026-08-28.")
)
```

`str_subset()` from stringr keeps messages that match a pattern. The `messages`
argument supplies the text. The `fixed("café")` argument treats `"café"` as
ordinary text rather than a regular expression.

`fixed()` is a good choice when the exact word, phrase, label, or punctuation
is already known. It prevents punctuation from acquiring a special
pattern-matching meaning.

### Ask a yes-or-no question

The support worker will eventually need one answer for every message.
`str_detect()` asks whether each message contains a match, returning `TRUE` for
yes and `FALSE` for no. We will display the answer in a table.

```{r}
has_order_prefix <- str_detect(messages, fixed("R-"))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    message = messages,
    contains_R_dash = has_order_prefix
  ),
  col.names = c("Message", "Contains R-"),
  caption = "Which messages contain R-?",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(has_order_prefix, c(FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE))
)
```

Only the third message contains `"R-"`. The search found the likely message,
but the rule does not require a complete order ID. It also accepts `"R-"`
without subsequent digits.

## Describe a set of matches

The two visible order numbers have the same structure:

- the letter `R`.
- a hyphen.
- exactly four digits.

A **regular expression**, often shortened to **regex**, is a compact
description of a text pattern. The next expression asks for the whole order ID
rather than its first two characters.

```{r}
order_id_pattern <- r"(\bR-[0-9]{4}\b)"

order_ids_by_message <- str_extract_all(
  messages,
  order_id_pattern
)

order_ids_by_message
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(order_ids_by_message[[3]], c("R-1042", "R-1043")),
  identical(sum(lengths(order_ids_by_message)), 2L)
)
```

The output groups results by message. An empty entry means that the pattern
found no order number in that message. The third entry contains the two IDs
visible in the example set.

Read this pattern from left to right:

| Part | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `\b` | Start or end at a word boundary. |
| `R-` | Match these two characters exactly. |
| `[0-9]` | Match one ASCII digit from 0 through 9. |
| `{4}` | Require the previous item four times. |
| `\b` | Stop at another word boundary. |

: Parts of the order ID pattern

R's raw string notation, written here as `r"(...)"`, keeps the backslashes
readable. Without raw notation, R requires
`"\\bR-[0-9]{4}\\b"`.

The order system defines its IDs with ASCII digits. In the ICU engine used by
stringr, `\d` also matches decimal digits from other writing systems. Using
`[0-9]` makes the rule explicit.

## Find several kinds of information

The messages also contain a date and an email address. Each information type
uses a separate pattern.

```{r}
date_pattern <- r"(\b[0-9]{4}-[0-9]{2}-[0-9]{2}\b)"
email_pattern <- r"([[:alnum:]._%+-]+@[[:alnum:].-]+\.[[:alpha:]]{2,})"

message_table <- tibble(
  message_number = seq_along(messages),
  message_text = messages
)

extracted_summary <- message_table |>
  mutate(
    order_ids = str_extract_all(
      message_text,
      order_id_pattern
    ),
    first_date = str_extract(
      message_text,
      date_pattern
    ),
    first_email = str_extract(
      message_text,
      email_pattern
    )
  )

extracted_for_display <- extracted_summary |>
  mutate(
    order_ids = map_chr(
      order_ids,
      \(ids) str_c(ids, collapse = ", ")
    ),
    order_ids = if_else(order_ids == "", "No match", order_ids),
    first_date = coalesce(first_date, "No match"),
    first_email = coalesce(first_email, "No match")
  )
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  extracted_for_display,
  col.names = c(
    "Message",
    "Text",
    "Order IDs",
    "First date",
    "First email"
  ),
  caption = "Matches kept with the message that supplied them",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    extracted_summary$message_number,
    seq_along(messages)
  ),
  identical(
    extracted_summary$message_text,
    messages
  ),
  identical(
    extracted_summary$order_ids,
    list(
      character(),
      character(),
      c("R-1042", "R-1043"),
      character(),
      character()
    )
  ),
  identical(
    extracted_summary$first_date,
    c(NA, NA, NA, "2026-08-28", NA)
  ),
  identical(
    extracted_summary$first_email,
    c(NA, "support@example.com", NA, NA, NA)
  ),
  identical(
    extracted_for_display$order_ids,
    c("No match", "No match", "R-1042, R-1043", "No match", "No match")
  )
)
```

The table keeps every match beside the message that supplied it. The underlying
`order_ids` column is a **list-column** because each message can produce zero,
one, or several IDs. The display copy converts each small character vector to
readable text and prints `No match` where the extractor found nothing.

`str_extract()` returns only the first match, which is why the other two columns
are named `first_date` and `first_email`.

`message_number` is a display position, not a durable identifier. Reordering
the vector would change it. Records from a real system should keep the source's
message ID from the moment they are read.

The email pattern has limited coverage. It recognizes the address in this
example, but it does not validate every email address that is valid under internet
standards. Finding text that resembles an email and proving that an address is
valid are different tasks.

## Use the start and end of a string

A loose match can occur in the wrong place. Some labels matter only at the
start of a text value, and some values must occupy the whole string. In these
single-line examples, `^` means "the start of the string" and `$` means "the
end of the string."

```{r}
log_lines <- c(
  "ERROR: file not found",
  "INFO: job started",
  "ERRORISH: not an error record"
)

error_lines <- str_subset(log_lines, "^ERROR:")

error_lines
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(error_lines, "ERROR: file not found")
)
```

The pattern requires the complete label `ERROR:` at the start. It excludes
`ERRORISH`, whose opening text and punctuation do not meet that rule.

Using both anchors requires a complete match from beginning to end. The next
pattern also uses parentheses to capture the year, month, and day separately.

```{r}
complete_date_pattern <- r"(^([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2})-([0-9]{2})$)"
date_inputs <- c(
  "2026-08-28",
  "2026-8-28",
  "due 2026-08-28"
)

date_parts <- str_match(
  date_inputs,
  complete_date_pattern
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    input = date_inputs,
    complete_match = date_parts[, 1],
    year = date_parts[, 2],
    month = date_parts[, 3],
    day = date_parts[, 4]
  ),
  col.names = c("Input", "Complete match", "Year", "Month", "Day"),
  caption = "Complete-date checks",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    unname(date_parts[1, 2:4]),
    c("2026", "08", "28")
  ),
  all(is.na(date_parts[2:3, 1]))
)
```

`NA` means "missing" in R. The last two inputs do not have the required
four-digit year, two-digit month, and two-digit day as a complete value.

This pattern requires the stated arrangement of digits. It applies no calendar check.
For example, `2026-99-99` has the expected shape but is not a real date.

## Replace matching text

The worker may need to share an example without the sender's address.
The following code substitutes `[email]` for the matching address before
sharing.

```{r}
redaction_report <- message_table |>
  mutate(
    removed_addresses = str_extract_all(
      message_text,
      email_pattern
    ),
    shared_version = str_replace_all(
      message_text,
      email_pattern,
      "[email]"
    ),
    changed = shared_version != message_text
  )

changed_messages <- sum(redaction_report$changed)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  redaction_report |>
    select(message_number, changed, shared_version),
  col.names = c("Message", "Changed", "Version to share"),
  caption = "Which messages the redaction step altered",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    redaction_report$shared_version[2],
    "Email [email] before 17:30."
  ),
  identical(
    redaction_report$removed_addresses[[2]],
    "support@example.com"
  ),
  all(lengths(redaction_report$removed_addresses[-2]) == 0L),
  !any(str_detect(redaction_report$shared_version, fixed("@"))),
  identical(changed_messages, 1L)
)
```

The report also keeps the removed text for inspection:

```{r}
removed_addresses <- redaction_report$removed_addresses |>
  list_c()

removed_addresses
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(removed_addresses, "support@example.com"),
  identical(
    sum(lengths(redaction_report$removed_addresses)),
    length(removed_addresses)
  )
)
```

The code changed one message and removed one address. The output shows both
counts and the removed text. An output-only report cannot show whether a
redaction pattern removed too much text.

Read the removed material. Count the removed matches. Compare that count with
the number of matches the pattern found.

The address is gone, while the rest of each sentence stays unchanged. One
successful example is not enough to establish that a redaction method protects
private information. Run checks on varied cases. Examine the result.
Follow the privacy rules that apply to the real records.

## Create safety checks from examples

Before searching the full inbox, the worker adds similar invalid inputs beside
the valid matches. The order ID must contain one `R`, one hyphen, and exactly four
digits. `mutate()` from dplyr adds the actual test result as a new column.

```{r}
id_cases <- tibble(
  input = c(
    "R-0001",
    "prefix R-1234 suffix",
    "R-12",
    "RR-1234",
    "R-12345"
  ),
  expected = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

id_cases <- id_cases |>
  mutate(actual = str_detect(input, order_id_pattern))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  id_cases,
  col.names = c("Input", "Expected", "Actual"),
  caption = "Expected and actual order ID results",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(id_cases$actual, id_cases$expected)
)
```

The expected and actual columns agree. Invalid inputs such as `R-12345` remain
visible during checks rather than becoming mistaken matches later.

## Reuse a pattern after these checks

After these checks, we place the extraction in a **function** that we can call again.
A function is a named set of steps that accepts an input and
returns a result.

```{r}
extract_order_ids_by_message <- function(text, pattern) {
  str_extract_all(text, pattern)
}

collect_unique_order_ids <- function(text, pattern) {
  extract_order_ids_by_message(text, pattern) |>
    list_c() |>
    unique()
}

ids_by_message <- extract_order_ids_by_message(
  messages,
  order_id_pattern
)
unique_order_ids <- collect_unique_order_ids(
  messages,
  order_id_pattern
)

unique_order_ids
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(ids_by_message, order_ids_by_message),
  identical(unique_order_ids, c("R-1042", "R-1043"))
)
```

The first function preserves one result per message. The second function
deliberately combines those results into a corpus-wide list and removes
duplicates. Its name makes the loss of message boundaries explicit.

The distinction matters when a later question concerns a match's source.
Keep the row-level result. Create a combined inventory only when the task
requires one.

## State which text the pattern accepts

Support messages may use accented letters or writing systems beyond English.
In ICU, `\p{L}` identifies code points classified as letters. The `\p{M}`
pattern identifies combining marks. A visible accented letter can consist of
a base letter followed by a separate mark.

```{r}
words <- c(
  "cafe",
  "café",
  "naïve",
  "李雷",
  "e\u0301",
  "hello-world"
)
letters_and_marks_pattern <- r"(^(?:\p{L}\p{M}*)+$)"

letters_and_marks <- str_detect(
  words,
  letters_and_marks_pattern
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false

knitr::kable(
  tibble(
    text = words,
    accepted_by_pattern = letters_and_marks
  ),
  col.names = c("Text", "Accepted by this pattern"),
  caption = "Checks of the stated letter-and-mark rule",
  row.names = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| include: false

stopifnot(
  identical(
    letters_and_marks,
    c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE)
  )
)
```

The first five examples follow the stated rule. The fifth displays as `é` but
uses `e` plus a combining accent. `hello-world` does not match because a hyphen
is punctuation. This check answers a specific text question. It is not a rule
for deciding whether a person's name or a word is valid.

::: {.callout-note}
## Technical detail: R has more than one pattern engine

A **pattern engine** is software that interprets a regular expression.
Different engines do not support identical features.

Base R uses POSIX extended regular expressions by default and PCRE2 when
`perl = TRUE`. The stringr package uses the ICU engine through stringi. These
engines share common syntax, but some Unicode rules and advanced features
differ.

The examples in this lesson use stringr for regular expressions. Run checks on a pattern
again if you move it to a different engine. Avoid `useBytes = TRUE` for normal
text because byte-level matching can split one UTF-8 character into several
pieces.
:::

## Apply the pattern after these checks

The support worker can use this process before searching the full inbox:

1. Write a few short examples that should match.
2. Add similar examples that must not match.
3. Use `fixed()` when you only need exact text.
4. Build a regular expression one piece at a time.
5. Examine the text you extract before replacing anything.
6. Record the expected answers in the lesson's hidden checks.
7. Add an example whenever the pattern produces an unexpected result.

## What to remember

- Use exact searches instead of regular expressions when they solve the problem.
- A regular expression describes a set of possible matches.
- Small hand-written examples make a pattern easier to understand.
- Expected failures are as useful as expected matches.
- Name the language and script that a pattern assumes. Digit and case rules
  differ between writing systems.
- Count the removed matches. Read the removed text as well as the retained text.
- A published example should stop the build when its result changes.

The pattern found both order IDs and removed one address. The report records
that removal. For each new pattern, keep examples that must match and examples
that must not match.
